analysis.one_liner: Cuts federal price supports for domestic sugar and loosens import quotas to lower consumer sugar prices.
analysis.headline: Despite 54 bipartisan cosponsors, the bill never got a committee vote and the federal sugar program kept operating as before.
analysis.plain_summary: The U.S. sugar program limits how much sugar can be grown and sold domestically, guarantees processors a minimum price through government-backed loans, and restricts imports. Together these keep U.S. sugar prices above world prices, which costs shoppers and food makers more every time they buy anything sweetened. This bill would have cut the guaranteed loan price, required import quotas set no higher than trade agreements demand, aimed supplies at keeping prices reasonable, and ended a program that has the government buy surplus sugar and sell it to ethanol producers.
analysis.who_benefits: American families who buy food with sugar in it, and the food and candy makers who use sugar as an ingredient, both pay inflated sugar prices under the current program. Lower guaranteed prices and larger, more flexible imports would push retail sugar prices down. Taxpayers would also save by ending the program that buys surplus sugar for biofuel producers.

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the guaranteed loan rate to 18 cents per pound for raw cane sugar for the 2015-2018 crops and lowers the sugar beet rate, reducing the price floor that props up domestic sugar prices.

Requires USDA to set marketing allotments — the caps on how much sugar each processor may sell — at levels that maintain adequate domestic supplies at reasonable prices, and allows USDA to suspend or modify the program considering the interests of consumers, workers, and businesses.

Requires import quotas to be set no higher than the minimum needed to comply with trade agreements, adjusted to target a stocks-to-use ratio of about 15.5 percent so prices don't become unreasonably high.
Repeals the Feedstock Flexibility Program, under which USDA buys sugar from processors and resells it to bioenergy producers, ending that taxpayer-funded purchase program.

analysis.who_pays: Domestic sugarcane and sugar beet growers and the processors who mill and refine their crop. They would face lower guaranteed prices, larger import competition, and the loss of the government sugar buyback program. Some marginal growers could see incomes fall or exit the business.

drawbacks.text: Cutting the loan rate and loosening import quotas would reduce revenue for sugarcane and sugar beet growers and processors, and the bill explicitly allows USDA to weigh the interests of agricultural producers when suspending program provisions.

Opponents of sugar program changes generally argue that opening the market wider to imports could leave the U.S. more dependent on foreign sugar, some of it produced under foreign subsidies, and could cost jobs in the domestic sugar industry. This argument is not addressed in the bill text, which simply lowers supports and expands import flexibility.
Repealing the Feedstock Flexibility Program removes a demand outlet for biofuel producers, who would lose access to government-purchased sugar for ethanol production.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's gains go to a broad, dispersed group — every household that buys sweetened food pays a few dollars more per year under the current program, and food manufacturers pay much more as businesses. Its losses fall on a small, concentrated group of sugar growers and processors concentrated in a few states. That imbalance is exactly why the program persists: the beneficiaries of the status quo are organized and the payers are diffuse. A fair accounting favors the reform, with the main caveat that abrupt cuts to grower supports could disrupt some farm businesses during the transition.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee, sent to a subcommittee, and never received a markup or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Joseph Pitts introduced the Sugar Reform Act of 2015 on March 26, 2015, with 24 original cosponsors from both parties.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture the day it was introduced, then on April 20, 2015 to the Subcommittee on General Farm Commodities and Risk Management.
It attracted 54 cosponsors — 40 Republicans and 14 Democrats — but the action history shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the rest of the 114th Congress.
The bill sat in committee until the Congress ended on January 3, 2017, meaning the existing sugar program — loan supports, marketing allotments, and import quotas — continued unchanged.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Domestic sugar growers and processors came out ahead: the price supports and import restrictions that keep their prices above world levels stayed in place, and consumers kept paying the difference. The House Agriculture Committee, which never scheduled action, preserved that arrangement without a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Sugar growers and the status quo

for.name: Rep. Joseph Pitts
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 24 original cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: 54 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan support but no path to a vote.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill; it sat in subcommittee for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Domestic sugar industry (growers and processors)
against.role: Sugarcane and sugar beet growers and processors
against.what_they_did: Actively defended the sugar program in farm bill and agricultural policy fights, opposing reforms that would cut loan rates and raise import quotas.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan — 40 of 246 House Republicans and 14 of 188 House Democrats cosponsored — but the bill never reached a vote, so no party-line roll call exists.

industries.industry: Domestic sugarcane and sugar beet growers and processors
industries.note: The current program's loan guarantees, sales allotments, and import quotas keep domestic sugar prices above world prices, so growers and processors profit at consumers' expense; this bill would have cut those supports. Its defeat preserved their arrangement.

industries.industry: Sugar-using food manufacturers (candy, baked goods, cereals)
industries.note: Sugar is a major input cost for these manufacturers, and U.S. sugar prices above world levels raise their costs and retail food prices. Lower loan rates and more flexible imports would have reduced both.
The bill repeals the Feedstock Flexibility Program, which has USDA buy sugar and sell it to bioenergy producers; repeal ends that channel and leaves taxpayers without the purchase program.
